content.text: The Open/Closed Principle doesn't forbid editing existing code. Robert C. Martin says so directly: it "doesn't mean you will never change the source code". It means arranging code so that expected kinds of change can be added with new code, without sweeping edits across modules that already work. Fix wrong code where it lives, and build extension points only where the same kind of change keeps coming back.
The shipping rule changes: orders of 500 or more now ship free. The team's guideline says OCP means existing classes are closed, so instead of editing
ShippingPolicy
, someone adds
ShippingPolicyV2
and registers it for checkout. The nightly invoice job still creates the old
ShippingPolicy
directly, so for a week invoices charge 30 for shipping that checkout showed as free. Meanwhile, adding a wallet payment method meant editing the same
switch
in checkout, refunds and reports: the one place where OCP would actually have helped.
The common misconception
The belief: the
Open/Closed Principle
means you should never modify a class once it's written. New behavior always goes into new classes: subclasses, decorators, V2s.

The wording invites it: "closed for modification" sounds absolute. Martin's own 1996 article said of a closed module: "The source code of such a module is inviolate. No one is allowed to make source code changes to it." His 2014 post states the essence as: "You should be able to extend the behavior of a system without having to modify that system." And Microsoft's architecture guide, in its section on single responsibility, says "Adding new classes is always safer than changing existing classes, since no code yet depends on the new classes."

The half-truth: code that lets you add an expected feature without touching working modules is valuable, and plugin systems prove it's possible. But that's a goal for specific kinds of change, not a ban on editing.
What actually happens
Meyer's "closed" meant stable and usable

Bertrand Meyer defined the principle in Object-Oriented Software Construction in 1988, and Martin's 2014 post quotes him. A module is open "if it is available for extension". It's closed when it "is available for use by other modules", which "assumes that the module has been given a well-defined, stable description". In other words, closed is about clients being able to rely on a module's interface. Craig Larman puts it precisely: a module "closed with respect to X" means clients are not affected if X changes.
Martin: "This doesn't mean you will never change the source code"

In 2013 someone on Twitter complained that OCP made little sense: presumably its fans barely use version control, since the only reason to change a source file would be bug fixes. Martin traced the confusion to his 1996 sound-bite, called it "a bit overstated", and pointed out that the same article says no significant program can be 100% closed and talks about strategic closure. Then he restated the principle: "This doesn't mean you will never change the source code, this doesn't mean you can stop using your version control systems (sheesh!)." The aim is that "when behavior changes in expected ways, you don't have to make sweeping changes to all the modules of the system", ideally "changing little or no old code".
Close against predicted variation, not everything
Larman argues that OCP is essentially the same as
Protected Variation

: "Identify points of predicted variation and create a stable interface around them." His advice is "You must pick your battles in design": apply it at the likely points of variation "but not others. Otherwise, effort is wasted and complexity may arise". He even notes that speculative future-proofing can cost more than reworking a simple design, and that intermediate developers tend toward overly flexible designs "in ways that never get used".
Wrong code is meant to be edited

Martin's 2020 summary of OCP explains what's actually protected: "When requirements change only part of the existing code is wrong. Much of the existing code is still right. And we want to make sure that we don't have to change the right code just to make the wrong code work again." A shipping rule that no longer matches the business is the wrong code. Wrapping it in a subclass keeps the wrong version alive.
The fix: edit the rule, close the real variation

✅ Right

content.text: The shipping rule is now one class with one current rule, so every caller, including the invoice job, gets the change. Payment methods are different: the team has added several, and each one used to touch three
switch
statements. Behind
IPaymentMethod
, checkout, refunds and reports are closed with respect to new payment methods. Adding one still edits a line of old code, the registration in
Program.cs
, which is exactly Martin's "little or no old code".

rows.text: OCP means never edit existing code
Martin: it "doesn't mean you will never change the source code"
A changed rule belongs in a new subclass
A rule that's no longer right is wrong code; edit it so every caller gets the fix
Meyer: closed means available for use by other modules, with a stable, well-defined description
Every class should be open to every extension
No significant program is 100% closed; Larman: pick your battles at predicted points of variation
Larman lists interfaces, polymorphism, indirection, and data- or rule-driven designs among its mechanisms

content.text: Look at the last few features of the same kind, like new payment methods or new report types, and count the files each one touched. If the same
switch
or
if
chain changes every time, you've found a point of variation worth protecting. If a kind of change happened once, editing was the right call.

blocks.title: V2 classes are duplication with extra steps

content.text: Keeping the old class next to a "fixed" subclass means two versions of a business rule, and any code that constructs the old one directly keeps the old behavior. Unless both versions must run side by side on purpose, for example during a gradual rollout, delete the old rule once the new one ships.
How to apply it in your project
When a rule changes or a bug is found, edit the code that owns it, with a test that pins the new behavior. That's not an OCP violation.
Search the history for features of the same kind that each touched the same
switch
if
chain or type check in several places.

items.title: Put a stable interface around that point

content.text: Use an interface and one class per variant, a lookup table, or rules read from configuration, so the next variant is mostly new code.
Don't add extension points for variations that haven't shown up. Revisit when a second or third change of the same kind arrives.
Key takeaways

items.text: OCP doesn't forbid editing code; Martin calls the "never touch it" reading an overstated sound-bite.
Meyer's "closed" means a module is stable and usable by others, so clients aren't disturbed.
Aim to add expected kinds of change with new code and little or no old code.
No program is fully closed: protect the points of predicted variation and pick your battles.
Wrong code is meant to be edited; wrapping it in V2 subclasses keeps the bug alive.
